entries.3588f3559786ba80c479adb32b7d1562701b01ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv102"/><title type="x-ms">Habakkuk</title> <div sID="gen20565" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20566" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">It</hi> is a very foolish fancy of some of the Jewish rabbin that this prophet was the son of the Shunamite woman that was at first miraculously given, and afterwards raised to life, by Elisha (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.18-2Kgs.4.37">2 Kings iv.</reference>), as they say also that the prophet Jonah was the son of the widow of Zarephath, which Elijah raised to life. It is a more probable conjecture of their modern chronologers that he lived and prophesied in the reign of king Manasseh, when wickedness abounded, and destruction was hastening on, destruction by the Chaldeans, whom this prophet mentions as the instruments of God's judgments; and Manasseh was himself carried to Babylon, as an earnest of what should come afterwards. In the apocryphal story of Bel and the Dragon mention is made of Habakkuk the prophet in the land of Judah, who was carried thence by an angel to Babylon, to feed Daniel in the den; those who give credit to that story take pains to reconcile our prophet's living before the captivity, and foretelling it, with that. Huetius thinks that that was another of the same name, a prophet, this of the tribe of Simeon, that of Levi; others that he lived so long as to the end of that captivity, though he prophesied of it before it came. And some have imagined that Habakkuk's feeding Daniel in the den is to be understood mystically, that Daniel then <hi type="italic">lived by faith,</hi> as Habakkuk had said <hi type="italic">the just should do;</hi> he was <hi type="italic">fed</hi> by that word, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.4">Hab. ii. 4</reference>. The prophecy of this book is a mixture of the prophet's addresses to God in the people's name and to the people in God's name; for it is the office of the prophet to carry messages both ways. We have in it a lively representation of the intercourse and communion between a gracious God and a gracious soul. The whole refers particularly to the invasion of the land of Judah by the Chaldeans, which brought spoil upon the people of God, a just punishment of the spoil they had been guilty of among themselves; but it is of general use, especially to help us through that great temptation with which good men have in all ages been exercised, arising from the power and prosperity of the wicked and the sufferings of the righteous by it. <div eID="gen20566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20567" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20568" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. The prophet complains to God of the violence done by the abuse of the sword of justice among his own people and the hardships thereby put upon many good people, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.1-Hab.1.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. God by him foretels the punishment of that abuse of power by the sword of war, and the desolations which the army of the Chaldeans should make upon them, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.5-Hab.1.11">ver. 5-11</reference>. III. Then the prophet complains of that too, and is grieved that the Chaldeans prevail so far (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.12-Hab.1.17">ver. 12-17</reference>), so that he scarcely knows which is more to be lamented, the sin or the punishment of it, for in both many harmless good people are very great sufferers. It is well that there is a day of judgment, and a future state, before us, in which it shall be eternally well with all the righteous, and with them only, and ill with all the wicked, and them only; so the present seeming disorders of Providence shall be set to rights, and there will remain no matter of complaint whatsoever. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv102"/> <div eID="gen20568" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20567" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sins of the People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 600.)</title> <div sID="gen20569" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The burden which Habakkuk the prophet did see. <hi type="super">2</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear! <hi type="italic">even</hi> cry out unto thee <hi type="italic">of</hi> violence, and thou wilt not save! <hi type="super">3</hi> Why dost thou shew me iniquity, and cause <hi type="italic">me</hi> to behold grievance? for spoiling and violence <hi type="italic">are</hi> before me: and there are <hi type="italic">that</hi> raise up strife and contention. <hi type="super">4</hi> Therefore the law is slacked, and judgment doth never go forth: for the wicked doth compass about the righteous; therefore wrong judgment proceedeth. <div eID="gen20569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20570" type="x-p"/> We are told no more in the title of this book (which we have, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.1">v. 1</reference>) than that the penman was <hi type="italic">a prophet,</hi> a man divinely inspired and commissioned, which is enough (if that be so, we need not ask concerning his tribe or family, or the place of his birth), and that the book itself is <hi type="italic">the burden which</hi> he <hi type="italic">saw;</hi> he was as sure of the truth of it as if he had seen it with his bodily eyes already accomplished. Here, in these verses, the prophet sadly laments the iniquity of the times, as one sensibly touched with grief for the lamentable decay of religion and righteousness. It is a very melancholy complaint which he here makes to God, 1. That no man could call what he had his own; but, in defiance of the most sacred laws of property and equity, he that had power on his side had what he had a mind to, though he had no right on his side: The land was <hi type="italic">full of violence,</hi> as the old world was, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.11">Gen. vi. 11</reference>. The prophet <hi type="italic">cries out of violence</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.2">v. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">iniquity</hi> and <hi type="italic">grievance, spoil</hi> and <hi type="italic">violence.</hi> In families and among relations, in neighbour-hoods and among friends, in commerce and in courts of law, every thing was carried with a high hand, and no man made any scruple of doing wrong to his neighbour, so that he could but make a good hand of it for himself. It does not appear that the prophet himself had any great wrong done him (in losing times it fared best with those that had nothing to lose), but it grieved him to see other people wronged, and he could not but mingle his tears with those of the oppressed. Note, Doing wrong to harmless people, as it is an iniquity in itself, so it is a great grievance to all that are concerned for God's Jerusalem, who <hi type="italic">sigh and cry for abominations</hi> of this kind. He complains (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.4">v. 4</reference>) that <hi type="italic">the wicked doth compass about the righteous.</hi> One honest man, one honest cause, shall have enemies besetting it on every side; many wicked men, in confederacy against it, run it down; nay, one wicked man (for it is singular) with so many various arts of mischief sets upon a righteous man, that he perfectly besets him. 2. That the kingdom was broken into parties and factions that were continually biting and devouring one another. This is a lamentation to all the sons of peace: <hi type="italic">There are that raise up strife and contention</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.3">v. 3</reference>), that foment divisions, widen breaches, incense men against one another, and sow discord among brethren, by doing the work of him that is the accuser of the brethren. Strifes and contentions that have been laid asleep, and begun to be forgotten, they awake, and industriously raise up again, and blow up the sparks that were hidden under the embers. And, if <hi type="italic">blessed are the peace-makers,</hi> cursed are such peace-breakers, that make parties, and so make mischief that spreads further, and lasts longer, than they can imagine. It is sad to see bad men warming their hands at those flames which are devouring all that is good in a nation, and stirring up the fire too. 3. That the torrent of violence and strife ran so strongly as to bid defiance to the restraints and regulations of laws and the administration of justice, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.4">v. 4</reference>. Because God did not appear against them, nobody else would; <hi type="italic">therefore the law is slacked,</hi> is silent; it breathes not; <hi type="italic">its pulse beats not</hi> (so, it is said, the word signifies); it intermits, <hi type="italic">and judgment does not go forth</hi> as it should; no cognizance is taken of those crimes, no justice done upon the criminals; nay, <hi type="italic">wrong judgment proceeds;</hi> if appeals be made to the courts of equity, the righteous shall be condemned and the wicked justified, so that the remedy proves the worst disease. The legislative power takes no care to supply the deficiencies of the law for the obviating of those growing threatening mischiefs; the executive power takes no care to answer the good intentions of the laws that are made; the stream of justice is dried up by violence, and has not its free course. 4. That all this was open and public, and impudently avowed; it was barefaced. The prophet complains that this iniquity was shown him; he <hi type="italic">beheld it</hi> which way soever he turned his eyes, nor could he look off it: <hi type="italic">Spoiling and violence are before me.</hi> Note, The abounding of wickedness in a nation is a very great eye-sore to good people, and, if they did not see it, they could not believe it to be so bad as it is. Solomon often complains of the vexation of this kind which he <hi type="italic">saw under the sun;</hi> and the prophet would therefore gladly turn hermit, that he might not see it, <reference osisRef="Jer.9.2">Jer. ix. 2</reference>. But <hi type="italic">then we must needs go out of the world,</hi> which <hi type="italic">there-fore</hi> we should long to do, that we may remove to that world where holiness and love reign eternally, and no spoiling and violence shall be before us. 5. That he complained of this to God, but could not obtain a redress of those grievances: "<hi type="italic">Lord,</hi>" says he, "<hi type="italic">why dost thou show me iniquity?</hi> Why hast thou cast my lot in a time and place when and where it is to be seen, and why do I continue to <hi type="italic">sojourn in Mesech</hi> and <hi type="italic">Kedar? I cry to thee</hi> of this violence; I cry aloud; I have cried long; but <hi type="italic">thou wilt not hear, thou wilt not save;</hi> thou dost not take vengeance on the oppressors, nor do justice to the oppressed, as if thy arm were shortened or thy ear heavy." When God seems to connive at the wickedness of the wicked, nay, and to countenance it, by suffering them to prosper in their wickedness, it shocks the faith of good men, and proves a sore temptation to them to say, <hi type="italic">We have cleansed our hearts in vain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.13">Ps. lxxiii. 13</reference>), and hardens those in their impiety who say, <hi type="italic">God has forsaken the earth.</hi> We must not think it strange if wickedness be suffered to prevail far and prosper long. God has reasons, and we are sure they are good reasons, both for the reprieves of bad men and the rebukes of good men; and therefore, though we plead with him, and humbly expostulate concerning his judgments, yet we must say, "He is wise, and righteous, and good, in all," and must believe the day will come, though it may be long deferred, when the cry of sin will be heard against those that do wrong and the cry of prayer for those that suffer it.
entries.2b3050d40264041a535e707edbfb011004ec4026: <div eID="gen20570" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgment Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 600.)</title> <div sID="gen20571" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Behold ye among the heathen, and regard, and wonder marvellously: for <hi type="italic">I</hi> will work a work in your days, <hi type="italic">which</hi> ye will not believe, though it be told <hi type="italic">you.</hi> <hi type="super">6</hi> For, lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, <hi type="italic">that</hi> bitter and hasty nation, which shall march through the breadth of the land, to possess the dwelling-places <hi type="italic">that are</hi> not theirs. <hi type="super">7</hi> They <hi type="italic">are</hi> terrible and dreadful: their judgment and their dignity shall proceed of themselves. <hi type="super">8</hi> Their horses also are swifter than the leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves: and their horsemen shall spread themselves, and their horsemen shall come from far; they shall fly as the eagle <hi type="italic">that</hi> hasteth to eat. <hi type="super">9</hi> They shall come all for violence: their faces shall sup up <hi type="italic">as</hi> the east wind, and they shall gather the captivity as the sand. <hi type="super">10</hi> And they shall scoff at the kings, and the princes shall be a scorn unto them: they shall deride every strong hold; for they shall heap dust, and take it. <hi type="super">11</hi> Then shall <hi type="italic">his</hi> mind change, and he shall pass over, and offend, <hi type="italic">imputing</hi> this his power unto his god. <div eID="gen20571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20572" type="x-p"/> We have here an answer to the prophet's complaint, giving him assurance that, though God bore long, he would not bear always with this provoking people; for the day of vengeance was in his heart, and he must tell them so, that they might by repentance and reformation turn away the judgment they were threatened with. <div eID="gen20572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20573" type="x-p"/> I. The preamble to the sentence is very awful (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold, you among the heathen, and regard.</hi> Since they will not be brought to repentance by the long-suffering of God, he will take another course with them. No resentments are so keen, so deep, as those of abused patience. The Lord will inflict upon them, 1. A public punishment, which shall be beheld and regarded among the heathen, which the neighbouring nations shall take notice of and stand amazed at; see <reference osisRef="Deut.29.25">Deut. xxix. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.25">25</reference>. This will aggravate the desolations of Israel, that they will thereby be made a spectacle to the world. 2. An amazing punishment, so strange and surprising, and so much out of the common road of Providence, that it shall not be paralleled among the heathen, shall be sorer and heavier than what God has usually inflicted upon the nations that know him not; nay, it shall not be credited even by those that had the prediction of it from God before it comes, or the report of it from those that were eye-witnesses of it when it comes: <hi type="italic">You will not believe it, though it be told you;</hi> it will be thought incredible that so many judgments should combine in one, and every circumstance so strangely concur to enforce and aggravate it, that so great and potent a nation should be so reduced and broken, and that God should deal so severely with a people that had been taken into the bond of the covenant and that he had done so much for. The punishment of God's professing people cannot but be the astonishment of all about them. 3. A speedy punishment: "<hi type="italic">I will work a work in your days,</hi> now quickly; this generation shall not pass till the judgment threatened be accomplished. The sins of former days shall be reckoned for in your days; for now the measure of the iniquity is full," <reference osisRef="Matt.23.36">Mt. xxiii. 36</reference>. 4. It shall be a punishment in which much of the hand of God shall appear; it shall be a work of his own working, so that all who see it shall say, <hi type="italic">This is the Lord's doing;</hi> and it will be found a fearful thing to fall into his hands; woe to those whom he takes to task! 5. It shall be such a punishment as will typify the destruction to be brought upon the despisers of Christ and his gospel, for to that these words are applied <reference osisRef="Acts.13.41">Acts xiii. 41</reference>, <hi type="italic">Behold, you despisers, and wonder, and perish.</hi> The ruin of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans for their idolatry was a figure of their ruin by the Romans for rejecting Christ and his gospel, and it is a very marvellous thing, and almost incredible. <hi type="italic">Is there not a strange punishment to the workers of iniquity?</hi> <div eID="gen20573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20574" type="x-p"/> II. The sentence itself is very dreadful and particular (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Lo, I raise up the Chaldeans.</hi> There were those that raised up a great deal of strife and contention among them, which was their sin; and now God will raise up the Chaldeans against them, who shall strive and contend with them, which shall be their punishment. Note, When God's professing people quarrel among themselves, snarl at, and devour one another, it is just with God to bring the common enemy upon them, that shall make peace by making a universal devastation. The contending parties in Jerusalem were inveterate one against another, when the Romans came and <hi type="italic">took away their place and nation.</hi> The Chaldeans shall be the instruments of the destruction threatened, and, though themselves acting unrighteously, they shall <hi type="italic">execute the righteousness of the Lord</hi> and punish the unrighteousness of Israel. Now, here we have, <div eID="gen20574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20575" type="x-p"/> 1. A description of the people that shall be raised up against Israel, to be a scourge to them. (1.) They are <hi type="italic">a bitter and hasty nation,</hi> cruel and fierce, and what they do is done with violence and fury; they are precipitate in their counsels, vehement in their passions, and push on with resolution in their enterprises; they show no mercy and they spare no pains. Miserable is the case of those that are given up into the hand of these cruel ones. (2.) They are strong, and therefore formidable, and such as there is no standing before, and yet no fleeing from (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">They are terrible and dreadful,</hi> famed for the gallant troops they bring into the field (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.8">v. 8</reference>); <hi type="italic">their horses are swifter than leopards</hi> to charge and pursue, and <hi type="italic">more fierce</hi> than the <hi type="italic">evening wolves;</hi> and wolves are observed to be the most ravenous towards the evening, after they have been kept hungry all day, waiting for that darkness under the protection of which <hi type="italic">all the beasts of the forest creep forth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.104.20">Ps. civ. 20</reference>. Their squadrons of horse shall be very numerous: "<hi type="italic">Their horse-men shall spread themselves</hi> a great way, for they shall <hi type="italic">come from far,</hi> from all parts of their own country, and shall be dispersed into all parts of the country they invade, to plunder it, and enrich themselves with the spoil of it. And, <hi type="italic">in making speed to spoil, they shall hasten to the prey</hi> (as those, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.1">Isa. viii. 1</reference>, <hi type="italic">margin</hi>), for they shall <hi type="italic">fly as the eagle</hi> towards the earth when she <hi type="italic">hastens to eat</hi> and strikes at the prey she has an eye upon." (3.) Their own will is a law to them, and, in the fierceness of their pursuits, they will not be governed by any laws of humanity, equity, or honour: <hi type="italic">Their judgment and their dignity shall proceed of themselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.1.7">v. 7</reference>. Appetite and passion rule them, and not reason nor conscience. Their principle is, <hi type="italic">Quicquid libet, licet</hi>—<hi type="italic">My will is my law.</hi> And, <hi type="italic">Sic volo, sic jubeo; stat pro ratione voluntas—This is my wish, this is my command; it shall be done because I choose it.</hi> What favour can be hoped for from such an enemy? Note, Those who have been unjust and unmerciful, among whom <hi type="italic">the law is slacked, and judgment doth not go forth,</hi> will justly be paid in their own coin and fall into the hands of those who will deal unjustly and unmercifully with them. <div eID="gen20575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20576" type="x-p"/> 2. A prophecy of the terrible execution that shall be made by this terrible nation: <hi type="italic">They shall march through the breadth of the earth</hi> (so it may be read); for in a little time the Chaldean forces subdued all the nations in those parts, so that they seemed to have conquered the world; they overran Asia and part of Africa. Or, through the breadth of <hi type="italic">the land</hi> of Israel, which was wholly laid waste by them. It is here foretold, (1.) That they shall seize all as their own that they can lay their hands on. They shall come to <hi type="italic">possess the dwelling-places that are not theirs,</hi> which they have no right to, but that which their sword gives them. (2.) That they shall push on the war with all possible vigour: <hi type="italic">They shall all come for violence</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.9">v. 9</reference>), not to determine any disputed right by the sword, but, right or wrong, to enrich themselves with the spoil. <hi type="italic">Their faces shall sup up as the east wind;</hi> their very countenances shall be so fierce and frightful that a look will serve to make them masters of all they have a mind to; so that they shall <hi type="italic">swallow up</hi> all, as the east wind nips and blasts the buds and flowers. <hi type="italic">Their faces shall look towards the east</hi> (so some read it); they shall still have an eye to their own country, which lay eastward from Judea, and all the spoil they seize they shall remit thither. (3.) That they shall take a vast number of prisoners, and send them into Babylon: <hi type="italic">They shall gather the captivity as the sand</hi> for multitude, and shall never know when they have enough, as long as there are any more to be had. (4.) That they shall make nothing of the opposition that is given to them, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.10">v. 10</reference>. Do the distressed Jews depend upon their great men to make a stand, and with their wisdom and courage to give check to the victorious arms of the Chaldeans? Alas! they will make nothing of them. <hi type="italic">They shall scoff</hi> (he shall, so it is in the original, meaning Nebuchadnezzar, who being puffed up with his successes, shall scoff) <hi type="italic">at the kings</hi> and commanders of the forces that think to make head against him; and <hi type="italic">the princes shall be a scorn to them,</hi> so unequal a match shall they appear to be. Do they depend upon their garrisons and fortified towns? <hi type="italic">He shall deride every stronghold,</hi> for to him it shall be weak, and <hi type="italic">he shall heap dust, and take it;</hi> a little soil, thrown up for ramparts, shall serve to give him all the advantage against them that he can desire; he shall make but a jest of them, and a sport of taking them. (5.) By all this he shall be puffed up with an intolerable pride, which shall be his destruction (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then shall his mind change</hi> for the worse. The spirit both of the people and of the king shall grow more haughty and insolent. Those that will not be content with their own rights will not be content when they have made themselves masters of other people's rights too; but as the condition rises the mind rises too. This victorious king shall <hi type="italic">pass over</hi> all the bounds of reason, equity, and modesty, and break through all their bonds, and thereby <hi type="italic">he shall offend,</hi> shall make God his enemy, and so prepare ruin for himself by <hi type="italic">imputing this his power to his god,</hi> whereas he had it from the God of Israel. <hi type="italic">Bel</hi> and <hi type="italic">Nebo</hi> were the gods of the Chaldeans, and to them they gave the glory of their successes; they were hardened in their idolatry, and blasphemously argued that because they had conquered Israel their gods were too strong for the God of Israel. Note, It is a great offence (and the common offence of proud people) to take that glory to ourselves, or to give it to gods of our own making, which is due to the living and true God only. These closing words of the sentence give a glimpse of comfort to the afflicted people of God; it is to be hoped that they will change their minds, and grow better, and ripen for deliverance; and they did so. However, their enemies will change their minds, and grow worse, and ripen for destruction, which will inevitably come in God's due time; for a haughty spirit, lifted up against God, <hi type="italic">goes before a fall.</hi>
entries.37faad1bcc9f021e409f0d130e5dbfe3b8d3a8d7: <div eID="gen20576" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prophet's Plea; The Prophet's Complaint. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 600.)</title> <div sID="gen20577" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> <hi type="italic">Art</hi> thou not from everlasting, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> my God, mine Holy One? we shall not die<hi type="small-caps">. O Lord</hi> , thou hast ordained them for judgment; and, O mighty God, thou hast established them for correction. <hi type="super">13</hi> <hi type="italic">Thou art</hi> of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity: wherefore lookest thou upon them that deal treacherously, <hi type="italic">and</hi> holdest thy tongue when the wicked devoureth <hi type="italic">the man that is</hi> more righteous than he? <hi type="super">14</hi> And makest men as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, <hi type="italic">that have</hi> no ruler over them? <hi type="super">15</hi> They take up all of them with the angle, they catch them in their net, and gather them in their drag: therefore they rejoice and are glad. <hi type="super">16</hi> Therefore they sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag; because by them their portion <hi type="italic">is</hi> fat, and their meat plenteous. <hi type="super">17</hi> Shall they therefore empty their net, and not spare continually to slay the nations? <div eID="gen20577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20578" type="x-p"/> The prophet, having received of the Lord that which he was to deliver to the people, now turns to God, and again addresses himself to him for the ease of his own mind under the burden which he saw. And still he is full of complaints. If he look about him, he sees nothing but violence done by Israel; if he look before him, he sees nothing but violence done against Israel; and it is hard to say which is the more melancholy sight. His thoughts of both he pours out before the Lord. It is our duty to be affected both with the iniquities and with the calamities of the church of God and of the times and places wherein we live; but we must take heed lest we grow peevish in our resentments, and carry them too far, so as to entertain any hard thoughts of God, or lose the comfort of our communion with him. The world is bad, and always was so, and will be so; it is out of our power to mend it; but we are sure that God governs the world, and will bring glory to himself out of all, and therefore we must resolve to make the best of it, must be ourselves better, and long for the better world. The prospect of the prevalence of the Chaldeans drives the prophet to his knees, and he takes the liberty to plead with God concerning it. In his plea we may observe, <div eID="gen20578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20579" type="x-p"/> I. The truths which he lays down, which he resolves to abide by, and with which he endeavours to comfort himself and his friends, under the growing threatening power of the Chaldeans; and they will furnish us with pleasing considerations for our support in the like case. <div eID="gen20579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20580" type="x-p"/> 1. However it be, yet God is <hi type="italic">the Lord our God,</hi> and <hi type="italic">our Holy One.</hi> The victorious Chaldeans impute their power to their idols, but we are taught to tell them that the <hi type="italic">God of Israel is the true God, the living God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.10.10-Jer.10.11">Jer. x. 10, 11</reference>. (1.) He is <hi type="italic">Jehovah,</hi> the fountain of all being, power, and perfection. <hi type="italic">Our rock</hi> is not <hi type="italic">as theirs.</hi> (2.) "He is <hi type="italic">my God.</hi>" He speaks in the people's name; every Israelite may say, "He is <hi type="italic">mine.</hi> Though we are thus sore broken, and <hi type="italic">all this has come upon us, yet have we not forgotten the name of our God,</hi> nor quitted our relation to him, yet have we not disowned him, nor hath he disowned us, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.17">Ps. xliv. 17</reference>. We are an offending people; he is an offended God; yet he is ours, and we will not entertain any hard thoughts of him, nor of his service, for all this." (3.) "He is <hi type="italic">my Holy One.</hi>" This intimates that the prophet loved God as a holy God, loved him for the sake of his holiness. "He is <hi type="italic">mine</hi> because he is a <hi type="italic">Holy One;</hi> and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he will be my sanctifier and my Saviour, because he is <hi type="italic">my Holy One.</hi> Men are unholy, but <hi type="italic">my God is holy.</hi>" <div eID="gen20580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20581" type="x-p"/> 2. Our God is from everlasting. This he pleads with him: <hi type="italic">Art thou not from everlasting, O Lord my God?</hi> It is matter of great and continual comfort to God's people, under the troubles of this present life, that their God is from everlasting. This intimates, (1.) The eternity of his nature; if he is from everlasting, he will be to everlasting, and we must have recourse to this first principle, when things seen, which are temporal, are discouraging, that we have hope and help sufficient in a god that is not seen, that is eternal. "Art thou not from everlasting, and then wilt thou not make bare thy everlasting arm, in pursuance of thy everlasting counsels, to make unto thyself an everlasting name?" (2.) The antiquity of his covenant: "Art thou not <hi type="italic">from of old,</hi> a God in covenant with thy people" (so some understand it), "and hast thou not done great things for them <hi type="italic">in the days of old,</hi> which we have heard with our ears, and which our fathers have told us of; and art thou not the same God still that thou ever wast? Thou art <hi type="italic">God, and changest not.</hi>" <div eID="gen20581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20582" type="x-p"/> 3. While the world stands God will have a church in it. Thou art from everlasting, and then <hi type="italic">we shall not die.</hi> The Israel of God shall not be extirpated, nor the name of Israel blotted out, though it may sometimes seem to be very near it; like the apostles (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.9">2 Cor. vi. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">chastened, and not killed; chastened sorely, but not delivered over to death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.118.18">Ps. cxviii. 18</reference>. See how the prophet infers the perpetuity of the church from the eternity of God; for Christ has said, <hi type="italic">Because I live,</hi> and therefore as long as I live, <hi type="italic">you shall live also,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.19">John xiv. 19</reference>. He is the rock on which the church is so firmly built that the <hi type="italic">gates of hell shall not, cannot, prevail against it. We shall not die.</hi> <div eID="gen20582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20583" type="x-p"/> 4. Whatever the enemies of the church may do against her, it is according to the counsel of God, and is designed and directed for wise and holy ends: <hi type="italic">Thou hast ordained them; thou hast established them.</hi> It was God that gave the Chaldeans their power, made them a formidable people, and in his counsel determined what they should do, nor had they any power against his Israel but what was <hi type="italic">given them from above.</hi> He gave them their commission <hi type="italic">to take the spoil and to take the prey,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6">Isa. x. 6</reference>. Herein God appears a mighty God, that the power of mighty men is derived from him, depends upon him, and is under his check; he says concerning it, <hi type="italic">Hitherto shall it come, and no further.</hi> Those whom God ordains shall do no more than what God has ordained, which is a great comfort to God's suffering people. Men are God's hand, the rod in his hand, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 14</reference>. And he has <hi type="italic">ordained them for judgment,</hi> and <hi type="italic">for correction.</hi> God's people need correction, and deserve it; they must expect it; they shall have it; when wicked men are let loose against them, it is not for their destruction, that they may be ruined, but for their correction, that they may be reformed; they are not intended for a sword, to cut them off, but for a rod, to drive out the foolishness that is found in their hearts, though they <hi type="italic">mean not so, neither does their heart think so,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.7">Isa. x. 7</reference>. Note, It is matter of great comfort to us, in reference to the troubles and afflictions of the church, that, whatever mischief men design to them, God designs to bring good out of them, and we are sure that <hi type="italic">his counsel shall stand.</hi> <div eID="gen20583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20584" type="x-p"/> 5. Though the wickedness of the wicked may prosper for a while, yet God is a holy God, and does not approve of that wickedness (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil.</hi> The prophet, observing how very vicious and impious the Chaldeans were, and yet what great success they had against God's Israel, found a temptation arising from it to say that it was vain to serve God, and that it was indifferent to him what men were. But he soon suppresses the thought, by having recourse to his first principle, That God is not, that he cannot be, the author or patron of sin; as he cannot do iniquity himself, so he is <hi type="italic">of purer eyes than to behold it</hi> with any allowance or approbation; no, it is that <hi type="italic">abominable thing which the Lord hates.</hi> He sees all the sin that is committed in the world, and it is an offence to him, it is odious in his eyes, and those that commit it are thereby made obnoxious to his justice. There is in the nature of God an antipathy to those dispositions and practices that are contrary to his holy law; and, though an expedient is happily found out for his being reconciled to sinners, yet he never will, nor can, be reconciled to sin. And this principle we must resolve to abide by, though the dispensations of his providence may for a time, and in some instances, seem to be inconsistent with it. Note, God's connivance at sin must never be interpreted into a giving countenance to it; for <hi type="italic">he is not a God that has pleasure in wickedness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.5.4-Ps.5.5">Ps. v. 4, 5</reference>. The iniquity which, it is here said, God does not look upon, may be meant especially of the mischief done to God's people by their persecutors; though God sees cause to permit it, yet he does not approve of it; so it agrees with that of Balaam (<reference osisRef="Num.23.21">Num. xxiii. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">He has not be held iniquity against Jacob,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">seen,</hi> with allowance, <hi type="italic">perverseness against Israel,</hi> which is very comfortable to the people of God, in their afflictions by the rage of men, that they cannot infer God's anger from it; though the instruments of their trouble hate them, it does not therefore follow that God does; nay, he loves them, and it is in love that he corrects them. <div eID="gen20584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20585" type="x-p"/> II. The grievances he complains of, and finds hard to reconcile with these truths: "Since we are sure that thou art a holy God, why have atheists temptation given them to question whether thou art so or no? <hi type="italic">Wherefore lookest thou upon the Chaldeans</hi> that <hi type="italic">deal treacherously</hi> with thy people, and givest them success in their attempts upon us? Why dost thou suffer thy sworn enemies, who blaspheme thy name, to deal thus cruelly, thus perfidiously, with thy sworn subjects, who desire to fear thy name? What shall we say to this?" This was a temptation to Job (<reference osisRef="Job.21.7">ch. xxi. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.24.1">xxiv. 1</reference>), to David (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.2-Ps.73.3">Ps. lxxiii. 2, 3</reference>), to Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.1-Jer.12.2">ch. xii. 1, 2</reference>. 1. That God permitted sin, and was patient with the sinners. He <hi type="italic">looked upon them;</hi> he saw all their wicked doings and designs, and did not restrain nor punish them, but suffered them to speed in their purposes, to go on and prosper, and to carry all before them. Nay, his looking upon them intimates that he not only gave them no check or rebuke, but that he gave them encouragement and assistance, as if he smiled upon them and favoured them. He <hi type="italic">held his tongue</hi> when they went on in their wicked courses, said nothing against them, gave no orders to stop them. <hi type="italic">These things thou hast done, and I kept silence.</hi> 2. That his patience was abused, and, <hi type="italic">because sentence</hi> against these evil works and workers <hi type="italic">was not executed speedily,</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">their hearts</hi> were the more <hi type="italic">fully set in them to do evil.</hi> (1.) They were false and deceitful, and there was no credit to be given them, nor any confidence to be put in them. They deal <hi type="italic">treacherously;</hi> under colour of peace and friendship, they prosecute and execute the most mischievous designs, and make no conscience of their word in any thing. (2.) They hated and persecuted men because they were better than themselves, as Cain hated Abel because <hi type="italic">his own works were evil and his brother's righteous. The wicked devours the man that is more righteous than he,</hi> for that very reason, because he shames him; they have an ill will to the image of God, and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> devour good men, because they bear that image. Though many of the Jews were as bad as the Chaldeans themselves, and worse, yet there were those among them that were much more righteous, and yet were devoured by them. (3.) They made no more of killing men that of catching fish. The prophet complains that, Providence having delivered up the weaker to be prey to the stronger, they were, in effect, made as <hi type="italic">the fishes of the sea,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.1.14">v. 14</reference>. So they had been among themselves, preying upon one another as the greater fishes do upon the less (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.3">v. 3</reference>), and they were made so to the common enemy. They were <hi type="italic">as the creeping things,</hi> or <hi type="italic">swimming</hi> things (for the word is used for <hi type="italic">fish,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.1.20">Gen. i. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">that have no ruler</hi> over them, either to restrain them from devouring one another or to protect them from being devoured by their enemies. They are given up to the Chaldeans as fish to the fishermen. Those proud oppressors make no conscience of killing them, any more than men do of pulling fish out of the water, so small account do they make of human lives. They make no difficulty of killing them, but do it with as much ease as men catch fish, that make no resistance, but are unguarded and unarmed, and it is rather a pastime than any pains to take them. They make no distinction among them, but all is fish that comes to their net; and they reckon every thing their own that they can lay their hands on. They have various ways of spoiling and destroying, as men have of taking fish. Some they <hi type="italic">take up with the angle</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.15">v. 15</reference>), one by one; others <hi type="italic">they catch</hi> in shoals, and by wholesale, <hi type="italic">in their net,</hi> and <hi type="italic">gather them in their drag,</hi> their enclosing net. Such variety of methods have they to destroy those by whom they hope to enrich themselves. (4.) They gloried in what they got, and pleased themselves with it, though it was got dishonestly: <hi type="italic">Their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous;</hi> they prosper in their oppression and fraud; they have a great deal, and it is of the best; their land is good, and they have abundance of it. And therefore, [1.] They have great complacency in themselves, and are very pleasant; they live merrily (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore they rejoice and are glad,</hi> because their wealth is great, and their projects succeed for the increase of it, <reference osisRef="Job.31.25">Job xxxi. 25</reference>. <hi type="italic">Soul, take thy ease,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.19">Luke xii. 19</reference>. [2.] They have a great conceit of themselves, and are great admirers of their own ingenuity and management: They <hi type="italic">sacrifice to their own net, and burn incense to their own drag;</hi> they applaud themselves for having got so much money, though ever so dishonestly. Note, There is a proneness in us to take the glory of our outward prosperity to ourselves, and to say, <hi type="italic">My might, and the power of my hands, have gotten me this wealth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.8.17">Deut. viii. 17</reference>. This is idolizing ourselves, sacrificing to the dragnet, because it is our own, which is as absurd a piece of idolatry as sacrificing to Neptune or Dagon. That which makes them adore their net thus is because by it <hi type="italic">their portion is fat.</hi> Those that make a god of their money will make a god of their drag-net, if they can but get money by it. <div eID="gen20585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20586" type="x-p"/> III. The prophet, in the close, humbly expresses his hope that God will not suffer these destroyers of mankind always to go on and prosper thus, and expostulates with God concerning it (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Shall they therefore empty their net?</hi> Shall they enrich themselves, and fill their own vessels, with that which they have by violence and oppression taken away from their neighbours? Shall they empty their net of what they have caught, that they may cast it into the sea again, to catch more? And wilt thou suffer them to proceed in this wicked course? Shall they not <hi type="italic">spare continually to slay the nations?</hi> Must the numbers and wealth of nations be sacrificed to their net? As if it were a small thing to rob men of their estates, shall they rob God of his glory? Is not God the king of nations, and will he not assert their injured rights? Is he not jealous for his own honour, and will he not maintain that?" The prophet lodges the matter in God's hand, and leaves it with him, as the psalmist does. <reference osisRef="Ps.74.22">Ps. lxxiv. 22</reference>, <hi type="italic">Arise, O God! Plead thy own cause.</hi>  <chapter eID="Hab.1"/> <div eID="gen20586" type="x-p"/>

entries.83c0bf64b117cc0a95390ae72d5f475b810a2f77: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12866"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen23986" type="x-p"/> Habakkuk, from a Hebrew root meaning to "embrace," denoting a "favorite" (namely, of God) and a "struggler" (for his country's good). Some ancient authors represent him as belonging to the tribe of Levi; others [Pseudo Epiphanius], to that of Simeon. The inscription to Bel and the dragon in the Septuagint asserts the former; and <reference osisRef="Hab.3.19">Ha 3:19</reference> perhaps favors this. Eusebius [Ecclesiastical History, 7.29] states that in his time Habakkuk's tomb was shown at Celia in Palestine.<div eID="gen23986" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23985" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23987" type="x-p"/> The time seems to have been about 610 B.C. For the Chaldeans attacked Jerusalem in the ninth month of the fifth year of Jehoiakim, 605 B.C. (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.1">2Ki 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.6">2Ch 36:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.2">Jr 46:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.36.9">36:9</reference>). And Habakkuk (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.5">Ha 1:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.6">6</reference>, &c.) speaks of the Chaldeans as about to invade Judah, but not as having actually done so. In the second chapter he proceeds to comfort his people by foretelling the humiliation of their conquerors, and that the vision will soon have its fulfilment. In the third chapter the prophet in a sublime ode celebrates the deliverances wrought by Jehovah for His people in times past, as the ground of assurance, notwithstanding all their existing calamities, that He will deliver them again. <reference osisRef="Hab.3.16">Ha 3:16</reference> shows that the invader is still coming, and not yet arrived; so that the whole refers to the invasion in Jehoiakim's times, not those under Jehoiachin and Zedekiah. The Apocryphal appendix to Daniel states that he lived to see the Babylonian exile (588 B.C.), which accords with his prophesying early in Jehoiakim's reign, about 610 B.C.<div eID="gen23987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23988" type="x-p"/> The position of the book immediately after Nahum is appropriate; as Nahum treated of the judgments of the Lord on Assyria, for its violence against Israel, so Habakkuk, those inflicted by, and on, the Chaldeans for the same reason.<div eID="gen23988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23989" type="x-p"/> The style is poetical and sublime. The parallelisms are generally regular. Borrowed ideas occur (compare <reference osisRef="Hab.3.19">Ha 3:19</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Ps.18.33">Psa 18:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.6">Ha 2:6</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.14.4">Is 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.14">Ha 2:14</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.11.9">Is 11:9</reference>).<div eID="gen23989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23990" type="x-p"/> The ancient catalogues imply that his book is part of the canon of Scripture. In the New Testament, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.17">Ro 1:17</reference> quotes <reference osisRef="Hab.2.4">Ha 2:4</reference> (though not naming him); compare also <reference osisRef="Gal.3.11">Ga 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.38">He 10:38</reference>. <reference osisRef="Acts.13.40">Ac 13:40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.41">41</reference> quotes <reference osisRef="Hab.1.5">Ha 1:5</reference>. One or two Hebrew words peculiar to Habakkuk occur (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.9">Ha 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.16">2:6, 16</reference>).<div eID="gen23990" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hab.1.1-Hab.1.17">Ha 1:1-17</reference>. Habakkuk's Expostulation with Jehovah on Account of the Prevalence of Injustice: Jehovah Summons Attention to His Purpose of Sending the Chaldeans as the Avengers. The Prophet Complains, that These Are Worse than Those on Whom Vengeance Was to Be Taken.</title> <div sID="gen23991" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12866"/><hi type="bold">1. burden--</hi>the prophetic sentence. <div eID="gen23991" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8e2c7248b9dfbd0d6aa252e07d2966fd1fe72b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12867"/><div sID="gen23992" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12867"/><hi type="bold">2-3. violence ... Why dost thou show me iniquity?--</hi>Similar language is used of the Chaldeans (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.9">Ha 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.13">13</reference>), as here is used of the Jews: implying, that as the Jews sinned by violence and injustice, so they should be punished by violence and injustice (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.31">Pr 1:31</reference>). Jehoiakim's reign was marked by injustice, treachery, and bloodshed (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.3">Jr 22:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.13-Jer.22.17">13-17</reference>). Therefore the Chaldeans should be sent to deal with him and his nobles according to their dealings with others (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.6">Ha 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.11">10, 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.17">17</reference>). Compare Jeremiah's expostulation with Jehovah, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.1">Jr 12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.20.8">20:8</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Job.19.7">Job 19:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.19.8">8</reference>. <div eID="gen23992" type="x-p"/>
entries.f38483776b0c201fc750a087b7a90c7d98420dba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12869"/><div sID="gen23995" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12869"/><hi type="bold">4. Therefore--</hi>because Thou dost suffer such crimes to go unpunished.<div eID="gen23995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23996" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">law is slacked--</hi>is chilled. It has no authority and secures no respect.<div eID="gen23996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23997" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment--</hi>justice.<div eID="gen23997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23998" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wrong judgment proceedeth--</hi>Decisions are given contrary to right. <div eID="gen23998" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e4072819c34d7268ddf701801050f503d2d7872: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12870"/><div sID="gen23999" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12870"/><hi type="bold">5. Behold ... marvellously ... a work--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.29.14">Is 29:14</reference>). Quoted by Paul (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.41">Ac 13:41</reference>).<div eID="gen23999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24000" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among the heathen--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Acts.13.41">Ac 13:41</reference>, "ye despisers," from the Septuagint. So the Syriac and Arabic versions; perhaps from a different Hebrew reading. In the English Version reading of Habakkuk, God, in reply to the prophet's expostulation, addresses the Jews as about to be punished, "Behold ye among the heathen (with whom ye deserve to be classed, and by whom ye shall be punished, as despisers; the sense implied, which Paul expresses): learn from them what ye refused to learn from Me!" For "wonder marvellously," Paul, in <reference osisRef="Acts.13.41">Ac 13:41</reference>, has, "wonder and perish," which gives the sense, not the literal wording, of the Hebrew, "Wonder, wonder," that is, be overwhelmed in wonder. The despisers are to be given up to their own stupefaction, and so perish. The Israelite unbelievers would not credit the prophecy as to the fearfulness of the destruction to be wrought by the Chaldeans, nor afterwards the deliverance promised from that nation. So analogously, in Paul's day, the Jews would not credit the judgment coming on them by the Romans, nor the salvation proclaimed through Jesus. Thus the same Scripture applied to both.<div eID="gen24000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24001" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye will not believe, though it be told you--</hi>that is, ye will not believe now that I foretell it. <div eID="gen24001" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ae94e0f64ebc3fae21cc1b34961643fa9565f35: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12871"/><div sID="gen24002" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12871"/><hi type="bold">6. I raise up--</hi>not referring to God's having brought the Chaldeans from their original seats to Babylonia (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.23.13">Is 23:13</reference>), for they had already been upwards of twenty years (since Nabopolassar's era) in political power there; but to His being about now to raise them up as the instruments of God's "work" of judgment on the Jews (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.6">2Ch 36:6</reference>). The Hebrew is future, "I will raise up."<div eID="gen24002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24003" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bitter--</hi>that is, cruel (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.42">Jr 50:42</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Judg.18.25">Jud 18:25</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.8">2Sa 17:8</reference>).<div eID="gen24003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24004" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hasty--</hi>not passionate, but "impetuous." <div eID="gen24004" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d92047b730bae9d655e921c991377a48a94cde6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12872"/><div sID="gen24005" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12872"/><hi type="bold">7. their judgment and ... dignity ... proceed of themselves--</hi>that is, they recognize no judge save themselves, and they get for themselves and keep their own "dignity" without needing others' help. It will be vain for the Jews to complain of their tyrannical judgments; for whatever the Chaldeans decree they will do according to their own will, they will not brook anyone attempting to interfere. <div eID="gen24005" type="x-p"/>
entries.992f830ce94281a7aa20bb9f7d3cc818dc67f2d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12873"/><div sID="gen24006" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12873"/><hi type="bold">8. swifter than the leopards--</hi>Oppian [Cynegeticks, 3.76], says of the leopard, "It runs most swiftly straight on: you would fancy it was flying through the air."<div eID="gen24006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24007" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">more fierce--</hi>rather, "more keen"; literally, "sharp."<div eID="gen24007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">evening wolves--</hi>wolves famished with fasting all day and so most keen in attacking the fold under covert of the approaching night (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.6">Jr 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.3">Zep 3:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gen.49.27">Ge 49:27</reference>). Hence "twilight" is termed in Arabic and Persian "the wolf's tail"; and in French, entre chien et loup.<div eID="gen24008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spread themselves--</hi>proudly; as in <reference osisRef="Jer.50.11">Jr 50:11</reference>, and Mal 4:2, it implies strength and vigor. So also the Arabic cognate word [Maurer].<div eID="gen24009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their horsemen ... come from far--</hi>and yet are not wearied by the long journey. <div eID="gen24010" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0fcca2f0540b314142ae117f677bbebe911de9e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12874"/><div sID="gen24011" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12874"/><hi type="bold">9. all for violence--</hi>The sole object of all is not to establish just rights, but to get all they can by violence.<div eID="gen24011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24012" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their faces shall sup up as the east wind--</hi>that is, they shall, as it were, swallow up all before them; so the horse in <reference osisRef="Job.39.24">Job 39:24</reference> is said to "swallow the ground with fierceness and rage." Maurer takes it from an Arabic root, "the desire of their faces," that is, the eager desire expressed by their faces. Henderson, with Symmachus and Syriac, translates, "the aspect."<div eID="gen24012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24013" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the east wind--</hi>the simoon, which spreads devastation wherever it passes (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.8">Is 27:8</reference>). Gesenius translates, "(is) forwards." The rendering proposed, eastward, as if it referred to the Chaldeans' return home eastward from Judea, laden with spoils, is improbable. Their "gathering the sand" accords with the simoon being meant, as it carries with it whirlwinds of sand collected in the desert. <div eID="gen24013" type="x-p"/>
entries.552b3f5c9e93d99ddbf89415bb3e11e2cc892dc4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12875"/><div sID="gen24014" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12875"/><hi type="bold">10. scoff at ... kings--</hi>as unable to resist them.<div eID="gen24014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24015" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall heap dust, and take it--</hi>"they shall heap" earth mounds outside, and so "take every stronghold" (compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.15">2Sa 20:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.32">2Ki 19:32</reference>) [Grotius]. <div eID="gen24015" type="x-p"/>
entries.2672b1b481cecd73b0e530f0644debfdb67883db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12876"/><div sID="gen24016" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12876"/><hi type="bold">11. Then--</hi>when elated by his successes.<div eID="gen24016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall his mind change--</hi>He shall lose whatever of reason or moderation ever was in him, with pride.<div eID="gen24017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall pass over--</hi>all bounds and restraints: his pride preparing the sure way for his destruction (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.18">Pr 16:18</reference>). The language is very similar to that describing Nebuchadnezzar's "change" from man's heart (understanding) to that of a beast, because of pride (see on <reference osisRef="Dan.4.16">Da 4:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.4.30">Da 4:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.31">31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.4.33">Da 4:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.34">34</reference>). An undesigned coincidence between the two sacred books written independently.<div eID="gen24018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24019" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">imputing this his power unto his god--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.5.4">Da 5:4</reference>). Sacrilegious arrogance, in ascribing to his idol Bel the glory that belongs to God [Calvin]. Grotius explains, "(saying that) his power is his own as one who is a god to himself" (compare <reference osisRef="Hab.1.16">Ha 1:16</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Dan.3.1-Dan.3.30">Da 3:1-30</reference>). So Maurer, "He shall offend as one to whom his power is his god" (<reference osisRef="Job.12.6">Job 12:6</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Mic.2.1">Mi 2:1</reference>). <div eID="gen24019" type="x-p"/>
entries.e017ad5855a969066060ba0d21e4c965bac846c7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12877"/><div sID="gen24020" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12877"/>12. In opposition to the impious deifying of the Chaldeans power as their god (Maurer, or, as the English Version, their attributing of their successes to their idols), the prophet, in an impassioned address to Jehovah, vindicates His being "from everlasting," as contrasted with the Chaldean so-called "god."<div eID="gen24020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24021" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my God, mine Holy One--</hi>Habakkuk speaks in the name of his people. God was "the Holy One of Israel," against whom the Chaldean was setting up himself (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.23">Is 37:23</reference>).<div eID="gen24021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24022" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we shall not die--</hi>Thou, as being our God, wilt not permit the Chaldeans utterly to destroy us. This reading is one of the eighteen called by the Hebrews "the appointment of the scribes"; the Rabbis think that Ezra and his colleagues corrected the old reading, "Thou shalt not die."<div eID="gen24022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24023" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou hast ordained them for judgment--</hi>that is, to execute Thy judgments.<div eID="gen24023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24024" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for correction--</hi>to chastise transgressors (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5-Isa.10.7">Is 10:5-7</reference>). But not that they may deify their own power (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.11">Ha 1:11</reference>, for their power is from Thee, and but for a time); nor that they may destroy utterly Thy people. The Hebrew for "mighty God" is Rock (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.4">De 32:4</reference>). However the world is shaken, or man's faith wavers, God remains unshaken as the Rock of Ages (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.4">Is 26:4</reference>, Margin). <div eID="gen24024" type="x-p"/>
entries.0e985de804ea762af2c076c6caf25f0989fa608f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12878"/><div sID="gen24025" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12878"/><hi type="bold">13. purer ... than to behold evil--</hi>without being displeased at it.<div eID="gen24025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24026" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">canst not look on iniquity--</hi>unjust injuries done to Thy people. The prophet checks himself from being carried too far in his expostulatory complaint, by putting before himself honorable sentiments of God.<div eID="gen24026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24027" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them that deal treacherously--</hi>the Chaldeans, once allies of the Jews, but now their violent oppressors. Compare "treacherous dealers," (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.2">Is 21:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.24.16">24:16</reference>). Instead of speaking evil against God, he goes to God Himself for the remedy for his perplexity (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.11-Ps.73.17">Psa 73:11-17</reference>).<div eID="gen24027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24028" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">devoureth the man that is more righteous--</hi>The Chaldean oppresses the Jew, who with all his faults, is better than his oppressor (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.51">Eze 16:51</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.52">52</reference>). <div eID="gen24028" type="x-p"/>
entries.b6c269198a3ccb9c5b3c4d1ba7a4f6a5975ae846: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12879"/><div sID="gen24029" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12879"/><hi type="bold">14. And--</hi>that is, And so, by suffering oppressors to go unpunished, "Thou makest men as the fishes ... that have no ruler"; that is, no defender. All may fish in the sea with impunity; so the Chaldeans with impunity afflict Thy people, as these have no longer the God of the theocracy, their King, to defend them. Thou reducest men to such a state of anarchy, by wrong going unpunished, as if there were no God. He compares the world to the sea; men to fishes; Nebuchadnezzar to a fisherman (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.15-Hab.1.17">Ha 1:15-17</reference>). <div eID="gen24029" type="x-p"/>
entries.a05845f88733d8de30dcca0152d32427380342e5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12880"/><div sID="gen24030" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12880"/><hi type="bold">15. they take up all of them--</hi>all kinds of fishes, that is, men, as captives, and all other prey that comes in their way.<div eID="gen24030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with the angle--</hi>that is, the hook. Some they take up as with the hook, one by one; others in shoals, as in a "net" and "drag" or enclosing net.<div eID="gen24031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24032" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore--</hi>because of their successes.<div eID="gen24032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24033" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they rejoice--</hi>They glory in their crimes because attended with success (compare <reference osisRef="Hab.1.11">Ha 1:11</reference>). <div eID="gen24033" type="x-p"/>
entries.33b24b485dcab73ad73f12819fc517452c84f891: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12881"/><div sID="gen24034" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12881"/><hi type="bold">16. sacrifice unto their net--</hi>that is, their arms, power, and military skill, wherewith they gained their victories; instead of to God. Compare <reference osisRef="Hab.1.11">Ha 1:11</reference>, Maurer's interpretation. They idolize themselves for their own cleverness and might (<reference osisRef="Deut.8.17">De 8:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.13">Is 10:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.24">37:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.25">25</reference>).<div eID="gen24034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24035" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by them--</hi>by their net and dragnet.<div eID="gen24035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24036" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their portion--</hi>image from a banquet: the prey which they have gotten. <div eID="gen24036" type="x-p"/>
entries.a65ab642557558d5dea2461d0c2a23cf21a47e4e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12882"/><div sID="gen24037" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12882"/><hi type="bold">17. Shall they ... empty their net?--</hi>Shall they be allowed without interruption to enjoy the fruits of their violence?<div eID="gen24037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24038" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore--</hi>seeing that they attribute all their successes to themselves, and not to Thee. The answer to the prophet's question, he by inspiration gives himself in the second chapter. <chapter eID="Hab.1"/>

entries.0bd9c1c61e850f3e2dfbbba7c0ffaa102269cf6a: <div eID="gen35057" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen35058" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35059" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35059" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35058" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35060" type="x-p"/> The prophet enters very abruptly on his subject, his spirit being greatly indignant at the rapid progress of vice and impiety, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.1-Hab.1.4">Hab 1:1-4</reference>. Upon which God is introduced threatening very awful and sudden judgments to be indicted by the ministry of the Chaldeans, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.5-Hab.1.10">Hab 1:5-10</reference>. The Babylonians attribute their wonderful successes to their idols, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.11">Hab 1:11</reference>. The prophet then, making a sudden transition, expostulates with God (probably personating the Jews) for permitting a nation much more wicked than themselves, as they supposed, to oppress and devour them, as fishers and foulers do their prey, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.12-Hab.1.17">Hab 1:12-17</reference>. <div eID="gen35060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35061" type="x-p"/> We know little of this prophet; for what we find in the ancients concerning him is evidently fabulous, as well as that which appears in the Apocrypha. He was probably of the tribe of Simeon, and a native of Beth-zacar. It is very likely that he lived after the destruction of Nineveh, as he speaks of the Chaldeans, but makes no mention of the Assyrians. And he appears also to have prophesied before the Jewish captivity, see <reference osisRef="Hab.1.5">Hab 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">Hab 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.2">Hab 3:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.16-Hab.3.19">Hab 3:16-19</reference>; and therefore Abp. Newcome thinks he may be placed in the reign of Jehoiakim, between the years 606 b.c. and 598 b.c. <div eID="gen35061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35062" type="x-p"/> As a poet, Habakkuk holds a high rank among the Hebrew prophets. The beautiful connection between the parts of his prophecy, its diction, imagery, spirit, and sublimity, cannot be too much admired; and his hymn, chap. 3, is allowed by the best judges to be a masterpiece of its kind. See Lowth's Praelect. xxi., xxviii. <div eID="gen35062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35063" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen35063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35064" type="x-p"/> The burden - המשא hammassa signifies not only the burdensome prophecy, but the prophecy or revelation itself which God presented to the mind of Habakkuk, and which he saw-clearly perceived, in the light of prophecy and then faithfully declared, as this book shows. The word signifies an oracle or revelation in general; but chiefly, one relative to future calamities.
entries.5e9e5247159d11ced7fa2734ab3a86f077960001: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen35064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35065" type="x-p"/> O Lord, how long shall I cry - The prophet feels himself strongly excited against the vices which he beheld; and which, it appears from this verse, he had often declaimed against, but in vain; the people continued in their vices, and God in his longsuffering. <div eID="gen35065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35066" type="x-p"/> Habakkuk begins his prophecy under a similar feeling, and nearly in similar words, as Juvenal did his Satires: - <div eID="gen35066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35067" type="x-p"/> Semper ego auditor tantum? <div eID="gen35067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35068" type="x-p"/> Nunquamne reponam? <div eID="gen35068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35069" type="x-p"/> Vexatus toties rauci Theseide Codri? <div eID="gen35069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35070" type="x-p"/> Sat. 1:1. "Shall I always be a hearer only? <div eID="gen35070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35071" type="x-p"/> Shall I never reply? <div eID="gen35071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35072" type="x-p"/> So often vexed?" <div eID="gen35072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35073" type="x-p"/> Of violence - The most unlawful and outrageous acts.
entries.484333a7cbc3413acad2312d134feff3b4b495df: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen35073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35074" type="x-p"/> And cause me to behold grievance - עמל amal, labor, toil, distress, misery, etc., the common fruits of sin.
entries.334b4234f372d20dfadd8834a9e59e8cc2d8da83: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen35074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35075" type="x-p"/> The law is slacked - They pay no attention to it; it has lost all its vigor, its restraining and correcting power, it is not executed; right judgment is never pronounced; and the poor righteous man complains in vain that he is grievously oppressed by the wicked, and by those in power and authority. That the utmost depravity prevailed in the land of Judah is evident from these verses; and can we wonder, then, that God poured out such signal judgments upon them? When judgment doth not proceed from the seat of judgment upon earth, it will infallibly go forth from the throne of judgment in heaven.
entries.63842db7525d520cfc12e8b5f4701970e4e8fd13: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen35075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35076" type="x-p"/> Behold ye among the heathen - Instead of בגוים baggoyim, among the nations or heathen, some critics think we should read בגדים bogedim, transgressors; and to the same purpose the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic have read; and thus it is quoted by St. Paul <reference osisRef="Act.13.41">Act 13:41</reference>. But neither this, nor any tantamount reading, is found in any of the MSS. yet collated. Newcome translates, "See, ye transgressors, and behold a wonder, and perish." <div eID="gen35076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35077" type="x-p"/> I will work a work in your days - As he is speaking of the desolation that should be produced by the Chaldeans, it follows, as Bp. Newcome has justly observed, that the Chaldeans invaded Judah whilst those were living whom the prophet addressed. <div eID="gen35077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35078" type="x-p"/> Which ye will not believe - Nor did they, after all the declarations of various prophets. They still supposed that God would not give them up into the hands of their enemies, though they continued in their abominations! <div eID="gen35078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35079" type="x-p"/> It is evident that St. Paul, in the above place, accommodates this prediction to his own purpose. And possibly this sense might have been the intention of the Divine Spirit when he first spoke the words to the prophet; for, as God works in reference to eternity, so he speaks in reference to the same; and therefore there is an infinity of meaning in his Word. These appear to be the words of God in answer to the prophet, in which he declares he will entirely ruin this wicked people by means of the Chaldeans.
entries.8a78df1b2019fa716e2f9b239e618a276f0de440: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen35079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35080" type="x-p"/> That bitter and hasty nation - Cruel and oppressive in their disposition; and prompt and speedy in their assaults and conquests.
entries.f8f7652075fcc94783aeaab6bae04230d413e530: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen35080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35081" type="x-p"/> Their judgment - shall proceed of themselves - By revolting from the Assyrians, they have become a great nation. Thus, their judgment and excellence were the result of their own valor. Other meanings are given to this passage.
entries.e161455beeefc922a27b3dbd04593669c3bf0273: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen35081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35082" type="x-p"/> Their horses also are swifter than the leopards - The Chaldean cavalry are proverbial for swiftness, courage, etc. In Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.4.13">Jer 4:13</reference>, it is said, speaking of Nebuchadnezzar, "His chariots are as a whirlwind; his horses are swifter than eagles." <div eID="gen35082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35083" type="x-p"/> Oppian, speaking of the horses bred about the Euphrates, says, "They are by nature warhorses, and so intrepid that neither the sight nor the roaring of the lion appals them; and, besides, they are astonishingly fleet." The leopard, of all quadrupeds, is allowed to be the swiftest. <div eID="gen35083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35084" type="x-p"/> The evening wolves - The wolf is remarkable for his quick sight. Aelian says, Οξυωτεστατον εστι ζωον, και μεντοι, και νυκτος και σεληνης ουκ ουσης ὁδε ὁρᾳ; "The wolf is a very fleet animal; and, besides, it can see by night, even when there is no moonlight." Some think the hyena is meant: it is a swift, cruel, and untameable animal. The other prophets speak of the Chaldeans in the same way. See <reference osisRef="Deu.28.49">Deu 28:49</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.40">Jer 48:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.22">Jer 49:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.17.5">Eze 17:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.19">Lam 4:19</reference>.
entries.e5142b701a38f0149854d60ceb81ed5236fcbae2: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen35084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35085" type="x-p"/> Their faces shall sup up as the east wind - This may be an allusion to those electrical winds which prevail in that country. Mr. Jackson, in his overland journey from India, mentions his having bathed in the Tigris. On his coming out of the river one of those winds passed over him, and, in a moment, carried off every particle of water that was on his body and in his bathing dress. So, the Chaldeans shall leave no substance behind them; their faces, their bare appearance, is the proof that nothing good shall be left. <div eID="gen35085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35086" type="x-p"/> Shall gather the captivity as the sand - They shall carry off innumerable captives.
entries.f0e7840f7c7c99e4bc0193767f37febab9b18bf6: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen35086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35087" type="x-p"/> They shall scoff at the kings - No power shall be able to stand before them. It will be only as pastime to them to take the strongest places. They will have no need to build formidable ramparts: by sweeping the dust together they shall make mounts sufficient to pass over the walls and take the city.
entries.6cc194c01c59623ac9fd9c165c4d9b835c8d348e: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen35087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35088" type="x-p"/> Then shall his mind change - This is thought to relate to the change which took place in Nebuchadnezzar, when "a beast's heart was given to him," and he was "driven from the dwellings of men." And this was because of his offending - his pride and arrogance; and his attributing all his success, etc., to his idols.
entries.e21ee694fabcbde57fd3912a40ee709a14d3f8c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen35088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35089" type="x-p"/> Art thou not frown everlasting - The idols change, and their worshippers change and fail: but thou, Jehovah, art eternal; thou canst not change, and they who trust in thee are safe. Thou art infinite in thy mercy; therefore, "we shall not die," shall not be totally exterminated. <div eID="gen35089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35090" type="x-p"/> Thou hast ordained them for judgment - Thou hast raised up the Chaldeans to correct and punish us; but thou hast not given them a commission to destroy us totally. <div eID="gen35090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35091" type="x-p"/> Instead of לא נמות lo namuth, "we shall not die," Houbigant and other critics, with a little transposition of letters, read אל אמת El emeth, "God of truth;" and then the verse will stand thus: "Art thou not from everlasting, O Jehovah, my God, my Holy One? O Jehovah, God of Truth, thou hast appointed them for judgment." But this emendation, however elegant, is not supported by any MS.; nor, indeed, by any of the ancient versions, though the Chaldee has something like it. The common reading makes a very good sense.
entries.0be0cba869b0f6f65aac0db077daad9cffe43620: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen35091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35092" type="x-p"/> Thou art of purer eyes - Seeing thou art so pure, and canst not look on iniquity - it is so abominable - how canst thou bear with them who "deal treacherously, and hold thy tongue when the wicked devour the righteous?" All such questions are easily solved by a consideration of God's ineffable mercy, which leads him to suffer long and be kind. He has no pleasure in the death of a sinner.
entries.61d05616ef9a1bf41c460c9d6a86a590de695bb7: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen35092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35093" type="x-p"/> Makest men as the fishes of the sea - Easily are we taken and destroyed. We have no leader to guide us, and no power to defend ourselves. Nebuchadnezzar is here represented as a fisherman, who is constantly casting his nets into the sea, and enclosing multitudes of fishes; and, being always successful, he sacrifices to his own net - attributes all his conquests to his own power and prudence; not considering that he is only like a net that after having been used for a while, shall at last be thrown by as useless, or burnt in the fire.
